comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Diagnosis on Preheim voltage drop issue:

Box 2 (590 D4) pulled.
Tested our cheap miliohmeter on the MEB_S3 and misc. busbars.
The tool: I'm not 100% convinced on the absolute values, which seem higher than should be expected even in a 'perfect' scenario... I think we can chalk that up to the quality of the leads. This Amazon special is like $130 total... Hioki leads by themselves are $250-$750.The tool itself is solid. Consistent, reliable readings, maintains it's 'zero' point, you can re-test the same connection after testing a few others and the value is accurate to the uOhm. So these values are useful compared to themselves, not to what we actually expect if we were measuring with a $2000 meter.

What I found is that there was a lack of contact at all three of the 'lateral' busbars (going from side-to-side on a module).

You can see this in the NOOXID pattern on the busbars. The module connections which had the worst values had the smallest area of NOOXID compression.

This is primarily due to insufficient material cut out of the protective housing on the 590s.  This caused the plastic to be .5mm-1.5mm proud of the terminal, causing the busbar to not make full contact. You could also see a small amount of plastic being smashed between the busbar and the terminal.

A secondary cause was excessive insulation on the busbars, which interfered with the plastic housing.

It wasn't pretty, but I was able to trim down the excess plastic using fine snips to where no further material was proud. I also trimmed back the insulation where necessary. This would be much more easily accomplished prior to installation.

Measurements were taken from internal-module-busbar directly adjacent to the desired joint to be measured. Meter was zerod to this value to reduce discrepancies relating to mating surface.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Troubleshoot voltage issue — work performed August 10, 2026
I set up the Vici VC480C+ micro-ohmmeter on the 20 mΩ range and verified its zero behavior by re-zeroing on a terminal-to-terminal placement and re-measuring each joint. Implied offset was 0.69 / 0.73 / 0.68 mΩ across spans of 1.19–1.92 mΩ, with no relationship to reading magnitude. Repeatability is ±0.025 mΩ. All readings below are terminal-zeroed.
I measured all three module-to-module busbar joints in Box 2 over two passes. As found: 1-to-2 at 1.23 mΩ, 2-to-3 at 0.46 mΩ, 3-to-4 at 0.72 mΩ. Ranking held across both passes.
I pulled the 1-to-2 and 3-to-4 busbars. The NO-OX-ID witness pattern showed partial compression on both. The orange terminal housing on the LYTH VDA590 sits up to 1.7 mm proud of the terminal face and was visibly crushed between busbar and terminal.
I trimmed the housing, applied NO-OX-ID and reinstalled each joint. On 3-to-4 I also found HV insulation fouling the joint face and removed it. 2-to-3 needed the housing cut down but no insulation trim.
Results

undefined
3-to-4 read 0.56 mΩ reinstalled dry, before insulation removal and NO-OX-ID.
Documented with 72 photos.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
TLDR: Anyone building 590s be very sure that these plastic housings are cut well below the face of the terminal.

We will need to pull the other two boxes to rectify. The other D4 will be a similar procedure to this box. The D8 will need to be disassembled to the point we can access the inner busbars.

Issues:
Very small brake fluid leak from the brake switch sensor. Brake sensor is functional but you have to get very deep into the pedal for it to engage. Might warrant replacement (did not come with new booster). There was no seal on the original I took off, but perhaps there should be one. Will get one.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Comment from yesterday:
"Installed rear shocks.
Attempted to adjust rear ride height.
Issues with vintage v-dubs IRS kit were discovered when attempting to adjust rear ride height.
Welds failing on swing plates adjustment blocks.
Torsion bar side of the adjustable swing plate not properly constrained to the backing plate, causing the plates to walk apart as the suspension moved. When I adjusted the screw this time it actually split the two apart completely. From the marks on the adjuster plate it looks to have been walking for a while.
The old shocks showed evidence of contact with the trailing arm.
Did a bunch of research to determine the best path going forward. As much as I'd just like to buy new spring plates and be done with it, they appear to be custom to this application and though I can find lots of parts that look similar I'm unable to determine compatibility. Every kit maker does this part a little differently. So we're best off fixing what we have.Had @Aharon Adams take a look at everything since he has the most torsion bar experience.
Plan going forward:
Remove spring plates. Straighten the plate and re-weld the adjustment blocks.
Add constraining hardware to ensure the two-part plate can't pull apart. The slot is there, but no matching stud or thread on the companion plate. Looking around it does appear to be something most high-quality kits do.
Add a bushing to the torsion bar cap to press the two plates together. This wasn't included in the kit but Aharon confirmed it's a necessity.
Install a longer adjustment screw to give us a little more height.
Regarding the shock mounting, I believe one of the many parts that were missing from the kit was upper shock mounts which were likely to prevent this contact. Where the shock mounts were intended to go I'm not sure. I moved the spacers around to create maximum clearance, and it appears that currently it will not make contact at full droop. Once we start driving it we can see if we need to address this. On the lift it seems OK."

comments.text:
@Marc Davis @Alex Noonan

@Billy Arrasmith and @Aharon Adams did a ride-along.

The possible halfshaft noise I was hearing is gone completely. Easy to replicate yesterday, today nothing. The rear suspension has settled about 15mm since yesterday after sitting overnight, sort of points to half-shaft angle as a likely cause.

Billy and Aharon both thought the front end actually feels pretty good on the road, especially with two people up front. Vehicle is ready to drive.

IMO doesn't feel great at highway speeds. Partially alignment, partially the aerodynamics.

Some notes from clickup/this morning.

There are two suspension components which need to be replaced. They have been reinstalled for now, but the new ones are on the way.
Lower arm - shock mount stud damaged from the extensive removal attempt.
Drag link - Seized in place, threads damaged during removal - air hammer slipped and hit between the nut and thread, my fault.
Front camber shim values are out of spec.
The lower torsion leaves have a divot which locates the grub screw, which locates the lower links. These were drilled about 4mm too far outboard either side of where they should be, resulting in an 'off the charts' shim arrangement. Maybe a mistake, maybe purposeful to gain more camber? I maxed out the shim adjustment and my quick camber measurement shows reasonable camber while unloaded.
There was big 'click' when we first pulled it out, didn't come back. Probably something settling, I'm going to retorque the grub screws and adjusters and test drive again to make sure it doesn't reappear.
The driver's side outboard halfshaft needs resealing. Billy knows about it.
The audio interference reappeared a little bit after reinstalling the ferrite filters. Not terrible, but not quite as good as it was. The combination is the same, but the locations have slightly shifted. If it's an issue I can dive back in.
Jordan Jones  [1:46 PM]
@Marc Davis @Alex Noonan
Vehicle is wiped down and ready to drive.

Driving much better than at any point in the past. No clearance issues, even with me and Billy in the front.

There are still a few creaks/squeaks. Some come from the body (front passenger door and rear doors), I think one is from the newly installed rear seat. There is an occasional creak that sound like it's coming from the rear drivetrain/suspension when accelerating. I'm going to leave these for now.

Possible halfshaft noise: I reported it was gone in the AM. After that, I raised the right rear by 10mm to level out the suspension. Noise returned. Lowered the rear end by 10mm again. Noise gone. Does seem to be halfshafts approaching their angle limit. I'm leaving it exactly where it is right now until Ferdman is gone, but there may be some more ride height tweaking in the future. Let's drive and see where it settles. (edited)

Picking this up. Summary of Thurs/Fri: Thu 7/16 — Aharon flagged adjustment asymmetry (passenger tight turning, driver easy/near end of travel); you attributed it to tolerance stacking, said re-indexing is limited by the wide plate. Driver-side vintageveedubs spring plate started deflecting again. Long deliberation on a permanent fix — confirmed no better off-the-shelf plate exists (Type E out on summer break), debated m16 studs+tap vs. through-bolt vs. m12. Decision: go m12, set ride height, then weld it solid. Aharon tacked brackets (washers down to m8), installed shocks at lowest setting with slight preload. comments.text:
Summary from today:
Unable to adjust ride height, and during arm replacement observed the torsion leaf stack ends no longer square. Attempted removal of torsion leaves for inspection: unable to remove leaves, jammed. Eventually able to hammer torsion leaves out and discovered the central keeper had stretched apart to the point where the torsion leaf stack had rotated and was no longer fully constrained in the center. This likely explains the crappy ride and, only the upper torsion leaf stack was actually supporting the weight, the lower stack was doing almost nothing. The upper torsion bar keeper was still intact, but was also stretching. And one final note, there are actually two leaves missing from each stack. Not sure if vintage v-dubs miscounted, or if they did that to change the spring rate. I'm going to add in the missing leaves when I reinstall.
I spoke with Nate a Wagenwest. He is rush shipping us a set of new central keepers. He actually said the slit is necessary for the torsion leaves to settle properly, but that the quality of the metal was very important. He asked where I got the beam from, and his response: "I could have guessed that"... he described vintage v-dubs as a bad company with "a long history of disasters". No surprise there...
As soon as the keepers come in I will put the front end back together.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Ryan brought the bus back from Soulspeed today reporting another inverter overtemp "limp mode" — an issue we hadn't seen in weeks since switching the reservoir return line from 3/8" to 5/8". I verified the basics first: coolant reservoir full and flowing well, no bubbles, and the coolant fan operating.
A few observations from digging in: the inlet and outlet are swapped on the inverter (probably doesn't matter, but we could set it to Tesla spec), and we run the inverter and motor in series while Tesla actually plumbs them in parallel. Neither seems likely to fix the inverter temp, but both are options to test.
I ran two controlled test drives at 100°F ambient to isolate whether airflow (the skidplate) is the culprit.
Run 1 (skidplate on): inverter started at 109°F and hit the 160°F overtemp limp mode after 13 minutes of hard-ish driving. Motor climbed from 163°F to 232°F — still mid-gauge in the Ampere GUI. Notably, the temperature creep is slow and steady, not "peaky" like Connolly was with its restrictive return line (30°F swings with throttle); Ferdman barely reacts to power input or off-throttle periods.
Run 2 (skidplate removed): inverter started at 104°F, motor at 165°F. Took 17 minutes / 2.5 laps of the same loop to hit limp mode at 160°F inverter, 241°F motor.
Conclusion: removing the skidplate bought roughly 25% more time/distance before limp mode, but didn't prevent it. Airflow is a contributing factor, not the root cause. Next candidates to test: correcting the inverter inlet/outlet to Tesla spec and re-plumbing the motor/inverter from series to parallel.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Claude:
"Fix cooling. Stop chasing signals.
Three reasons, and the third decides the order.
1. The bus has given up what it has. We now know the derate driver (motor temp), the inverter's limit and which sensor it uses (module, 80 °C), and the coolant temperature (RTD1). The remaining signal mysteries — hot-spot reading zero, the duplicated coolant field, AEM's channel labels — wouldn't change a single action. Chasing them further is bookkeeping.

2. The cooling system is already flat out and losing. Pump at 100 % duty and ~6,500 rpm for the entire evening — never modulated, no reserve. Module-to-coolant delta normal at 3.2 °C median. So heat transfer out of the modules is fine and the pump is maxed; the constraint is heat-rejection capacity, not control and not the interface.

3. Order matters — settings first would make it worse. Raising the derate thresholds hands torque back, which puts more heat into a loop that's already out of margin, while the inverter sits at its 80 °C limit. Cooling first isn't just safer, it's the only sequence that isn't self-defeating. And it pays twice: cooler coolant means a cooler motor, which backs the derate off on its own and gives you some torque back without touching a single parameter.

Start here — Fan1 is never commanded
Not once, at any coolant temperature, all the way to 65 °C with 40 °C ambient. Fan2 runs continuously. Either this car only has one fan wired to the Fan2 output, or there's a second fan that isn't being asked to run — which would be free capacity sitting idle. That's a five-minute check and it's the cheapest possible outcome.

After that, in cost order:
Airflow at the radiator— blockage, missing shroud, or hot air recirculating. At 40 °C ambient every degree of approach matters.
Loop topology— is the inverter fed before or after the motor? RTD1 is coolantbefore the inverterand it's already 62 °C. If a 129 °C motor sits upstream, the inverter is being handed pre-heated coolant and can never win. Worth confirming the plumbing order; if it is motor-then-inverter, re-routing or splitting the loop is likely the single biggest lever.
Radiator capacity— to hold modules under 70 °C you need coolant near 50 °C, which is only 10 °C above that day's ambient. That may simply be more than this radiator can do, in which case it's a sizing decision.
Actual flow— the pump is commanded 100 %, but air lock or a restriction would still starve it."
Me:
I'm not sure what is meant by 'modules'. Is claude confusing the motor circuit and the battery circuit? Claude is only looking at the motor circuit, correct?

Not sure what is referred to as 'fan 1' and 'fan 2', but I can confirm that all 3 fans come on as expected. There are currently two motor radiators, the original and the temporary secondary, both come on at the same time.
Airflow at both radiators is questionable. We have one small radiator horizontally under the car, and one in the cubby on the rear driver's side.
Inverter is fed before the motor. Circuit currently:
Pump > inverter > motor > secondary rad > ovar > primary rad > reservoir
Radiator capacity... I don't believe this is significantly different than any of our other cars.
Air lock or starvation. I see no evidence of flow restriction. In the reservoir there are no bubbles, flow looks good, level stays steady.




My thoughts...
Airflow on the primary radiator does appear to have an effect. Removing the skidplate increased the time-to-overheat by 25%.
Adding a secondary radiator did make a significant improvement in the symptoms with no other changes Prior to that change coolant temps were over 160F and the symptom was inverter overtemp errors and the vehicle shutting off. Adding a second radiator in a spot with minimal airflow temps dropped by 20F. Not enough to prevent derating, but better than before.
The differences between this car and our other cars:
SDU
Radiator placement

comments.text: Racked Ferdman and removed both rear shocks and shock mounts. Cleaned, sanded, and painted the shock mounts. While those dried, started on capturing the slide and spring plates. Began with an M8 through-bolt, but that didn't pull the plates close enough at 25 ft-lb — could still see light through the plates when shined from underneath. Moved to tapping the rear plate to M10, but on torquing realized I couldn't get enough clamp force, and "pulling" one plate to the other didn't seem sufficient on its own. Ended up drilling 10.5mm holes through all plates to allow the front plates to move as they came together, then sandwiched the plates together with M10 hardware torqued to 38 ft-lb. Reassembled with new shocks, painted shock mounts, and torqued the wheels.
